title: Beyond Referrals: Your Pipeline Readiness Score
subtitle: Measures how ready your financial services firm is to build a predictable, marketing-driven pipeline that does not depend on introductions.

questions.text: When you look at new client enquiries over the last 12 months, where did most of them come from?

answers.label: Introductions from existing clients or professional connections, with almost nothing else
Mostly introductions, with occasional direct enquiries we could not trace to a specific source
A mix of introductions and direct enquiries from content, search or our digital presence
Mostly direct inbound, with introductions as a secondary channel
A consistent stream of direct inbound from marketing, with referrals as a welcome addition rather than the main source

questions.text: If your three strongest referral sources went quiet for six months, what would happen to your pipeline?

answers.label: It would effectively dry up — we have no other channel generating enquiries
It would fall significantly and we would struggle to replace the volume in the short term
It would hurt, but we have some content and digital presence that generates occasional direct enquiries
We would feel it, but our direct inbound channel would absorb most of the gap
Minimal impact — our marketing-driven pipeline would continue independently

questions.text: How would you describe your firm's current approach to business development?

answers.label: It rests almost entirely on the network of senior partners and directors
We attend events and stay visible in the professional community, but there is no marketing channel behind it
We have a website and produce some content, but new business still comes mainly from relationships
We have a mix of relationship-led and content-driven activity, with a loose strategy behind both
We have a documented strategy with a production process behind it and track how each channel is performing

questions.text: How many new clients did your firm take on in the last 12 months?
questions.hint: Count mandates or engagements, not individual contacts.

questions.text: Of those new clients, roughly what percentage came through an introduction or referral?
questions.hint: Include warm introductions from professional connections as well as direct client referrals.

questions.text: How many hours per week does a senior partner or director spend on referral relationship maintenance: calls, coffees, networking events?
questions.hint: Include travel time and follow-up. If more than one person, use the combined total. This figure is used to calculate annual senior time on referral maintenance (weekly hours x 52 weeks).

low.headline: Your pipeline runs on introductions
low.text: Most financial services firms are in exactly this position. The risk is not obvious while the referrals keep coming, but a network that is not continuously replenished will eventually slow. The firms that move past referral dependency build a parallel channel that is already generating enquiries before the introductions thin out — not as a contingency, but as a deliberate second engine.
steps: Map where your last 20 new clients came from and note which sources you have any real control over
Identify the two or three questions your ideal clients are asking during the research phase — before they decide who to call
Publish one piece of content that answers each of those questions, in language your specific audience would recognise

mid.headline: You have started to diversify, but referrals still do the heavy lifting
mid.text: You have a direct channel and it is generating some enquiries. The risk is that the referral network is still the main driver, which means the direct channel has not been tested at scale. The research phase — the period when a prospect is reading and evaluating firms before they make contact — is where the real opportunity sits.
steps: Audit your last 12 months of inbound and note what prompted each contact, particularly the direct enquiries
Identify where in the research phase your content is missing — the questions being asked that you have not answered yet
Build a production process so publishing happens consistently, not only when there is time

high.headline: You are building the right kind of pipeline
high.text: Your firm is less dependent on introductions than most in this space. The enquiries arriving from your content or digital presence tend to come from people who have already done their reading — and that usually means stronger fit and better retention. The work now is to protect the consistency and make sure the content continues to reflect exactly who you want to attract.
steps: Review whether your content is speaking to your specific segment or to a broader financial services audience
Build in a quarterly review of enquiry quality to check whether the fit is improving over time
Track which content pieces are generating contact and produce more in those areas

questions.text: How often does your firm publish content — articles, market commentary, sector insight — that your target audience would find genuinely useful?

answers.label: Rarely or never
A few times a year, when there is something significant to say or time to say it
Monthly, roughly — but it depends on who is available and what is happening in the market
Roughly weekly, with a loose process behind it
Consistently, driven by a production process that runs regardless of who is available

questions.text: When your firm publishes content, what typically triggers it?

answers.label: A significant market event or regulatory change that forces a response
When a partner has capacity and happens to have something to say
A loose plan that gets disrupted by other priorities
An editorial calendar that is mostly followed
A production system with clear ownership that runs independently of individual availability

questions.text: How does your firm's content speak to the research phase — the period when a prospect is reading and evaluating firms before they decide who to call?

answers.label: We have not thought about content in those terms
We know the research phase exists but have not structured our content around it
Some of our content addresses those questions, but not consistently
We have mapped the questions our ideal clients ask during that phase and produce content that answers them
Our entire content strategy is built around showing up during the research phase, and we track how well it is working

questions.text: How would you describe the published point of view your firm puts out on the market, the sector, or the issues your clients face?

answers.label: We do not publish a point of view — our content is factual and stays neutral
We share market updates but avoid taking a clear position
We occasionally share our perspective but it is not a deliberate part of our content strategy
We have a clear point of view and publish it consistently across the topics that matter to our clients
Our published perspective is a central part of how we attract the right clients and filter out the wrong ones

low.headline: Content exists when there is time
low.text: This is the most common pattern in financial services. The point of view is usually there inside the firm — what is missing is a production process that makes publishing the default rather than something that happens occasionally. The firms that move fastest on this build the process before they feel the pipeline pressure, not after.
steps: Identify one person responsible for content output — not necessarily the writer, but the owner who ensures it happens
Set a sustainable cadence: one substantive piece per month is enough to begin building an audience
Write down the three questions your ideal clients are most likely to be asking during the research phase and treat those as your first content brief

mid.headline: You publish, but not predictably
mid.text: You understand the value of content and you have shown you can produce it. What is usually missing at this stage is the production process that removes the dependency on any one person's availability or enthusiasm. Consistency is not about volume — it is about a system that keeps running.
steps: Document your content process from brief to compliance to publish, even if it is only half a page
Build a content calendar six weeks ahead so you are not writing under pressure
Identify which existing pieces have generated the strongest enquiries and produce more in that area

high.headline: Content is working as a business development channel
high.text: Consistent content output is one of the harder things to build in this environment, given compliance requirements and the competing demands on senior time. If you are publishing reliably, the next question is whether the content is drawing in the right conversations and whether your point of view is specific enough to differentiate you from the rest of the sector.
steps: Track which content pieces are generating enquiries and note what they have in common
Check whether the tone and depth of your content reflects the level and type of client you want to attract
Consider whether your published perspective is distinct enough that a reader would know immediately this came from your firm

questions.text: How often does content your firm has commissioned or produced get significantly delayed or killed at compliance review?

answers.label: Frequently — it is a constant source of friction that slows or stops campaigns
Often — we lose significant time and sometimes drop campaigns entirely as a result
Occasionally — most content gets through but there are regular revisions that add time
Rarely — our marketing partners understand the environment and produce content that survives review
Almost never — our process is built around compliance requirements from the start, so surprises are rare

questions.text: When you brief a marketing partner on a campaign or content piece, how much of the regulatory context do they need explaining from scratch?

answers.label: All of it — every engagement starts with a compliance primer and significant onboarding time
A lot — most partners understand the basics but need extensive guidance on what is and is not possible here
Some — our partners have financial services experience but still need guidance on our specific requirements
Very little — our partners have worked in this environment and already know what compliance will flag
None — our partners anticipate compliance requirements before the work is reviewed and brief accordingly

questions.text: When regulatory guidance shifts and affects your website or communications, how does your firm respond?

answers.label: We are often slow to update — compliance and marketing are not well coordinated
We update reactively, which sometimes means content stays live longer than it should
We have a process but it takes longer than we would like to get changes made
We respond promptly — our marketing function stays close to regulatory changes and acts quickly
We anticipate regulatory shifts and plan updates in advance so we are never caught reactive

low.headline: Compliance is slowing your marketing output
low.text: This is a predictable result of working with marketing partners who do not understand the environment. Content that does not anticipate what a compliance function will flag gets revised repeatedly or killed entirely — which adds cost, erodes the relationship with the marketing team, and means your publishing calendar runs months behind where it should be. The fix is usually a specialist, not a longer brief.
steps: Track how much time each content project loses to compliance revisions and add that to your true cost of marketing
Brief any new marketing partner on your specific compliance requirements before work begins, not after first draft
Consider whether the cumulative cost of repeated revisions with a generalist outweighs the cost of a specialist who already knows this environment

mid.headline: Compliance is manageable but it still costs time
mid.text: You are not losing major campaigns, but the friction is there and it adds up. The difference between a marketing partner who already knows this environment and one who is learning it on your time tends to show in speed and quality — both of which matter when your publishing calendar depends on compliance sign-off.
steps: Track the average revision cycle for content pieces going through compliance review
Share past compliance feedback with your marketing partner so they build that knowledge in without repeating mistakes
Identify the types of content that consistently clear review quickly and build your calendar around them

high.headline: Compliance is part of the process, not a barrier
high.text: You have built the kind of working environment where compliance and marketing are not in friction. That is not the default in this sector and it is worth protecting — particularly as you increase your content output and the volume of material going through review.
steps: Make sure new hires and new marketing partners are briefed on your compliance process from day one, not after first submission
Document which types of content clear review smoothly and build your content calendar around those categories
Stay close to regulatory changes so your marketing function can anticipate updates rather than react to them

questions.text: How clearly does your firm's current website and content reflect the specific audience you serve — their language, their concerns, their typical situation?

answers.label: Our marketing could describe almost any financial services firm — there is little specific to our audience
It reflects our sector broadly but does not speak clearly to our specific client type
It is reasonably targeted but we know there are generic sections that do not represent us well
It speaks clearly to our audience, with content that addresses their specific situations and concerns
Every element of our digital presence is built around what our specific clients need to see before they hand over their trust

questions.text: When a prospective client arrives at your website, how confident are you that they will quickly understand whether your firm is the right fit for them?

answers.label: Not confident — our site is broadly descriptive and does not differentiate us clearly
Slightly confident — they would understand what we do but not who we are specifically right for
Reasonably confident — the message is there but it is not as immediate as it should be
Fairly confident — most of our target audience would recognise themselves in what we publish
Very confident — our site is built specifically to answer that question for the right prospect

questions.text: How different is your firm's visual identity, tone, and content strategy from the majority of competitors in your segment?

answers.label: Very similar — we look and sound broadly like the rest of the sector
We have some differentiation but it is not consistent across channels or materials
Our identity is reasonably distinct but does not always reflect the specific audience we serve
We have a clear and consistent identity that our audience recognises as specific to them
Our brand and content strategy are built entirely around what builds trust with our specific segment — not financial services broadly

low.headline: Your marketing describes the sector, not your firm
low.text: A website or content strategy that could describe almost any financial services firm is not doing the job. What a pension trustee committee needs to see before they hand over their trust is completely different from what an entrepreneur looking for acquisition finance needs to see. Generic positioning is not neutral — it actively reduces the quality of the enquiries you receive and makes it harder for the right prospect to self-select.
steps: Write one paragraph that describes your ideal client specifically: their situation, their typical concern, and what they are actually trying to solve
Audit your current website copy against that description and note every place it goes generic
Rewrite your homepage to speak directly to that specific audience, not to financial services broadly

mid.headline: Your positioning is directionally right but not specific enough
mid.text: You are not invisible to your target audience, but you are probably not the obvious choice either. The firms that attract the strongest inbound are the ones where a prospect reads the site and thinks: this firm works with people in exactly my situation. The gap between where you are and that position is usually smaller than it looks — it is a specificity problem, not a structural one.
steps: Identify the two or three situations your best clients were in when they first made contact with your firm
Check whether those situations are described clearly anywhere on your website or in your content
Produce one piece of content that speaks directly to that specific situation, rather than to your sector broadly

high.headline: Your audience recognises itself in what you publish
high.text: Specificity is one of the strongest signals of expertise in financial services. When a prospect reads your content and feels it was written for their situation, the conversion from reading to making contact tends to be stronger — and the fit at engagement tends to hold. The question now is whether you are protecting that specificity as you grow.
steps: Review whether your case studies and client outcomes reflect the specific segment you want to attract, not just the range of work you have done
Check that your visual identity and tone sit at the right point in the trust spectrum for your specific audience
Identify adjacent questions your ideal clients are asking during the research phase that you are not yet answering

cta.description: In 30 minutes I'll show you which two gaps to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing.
